Lab supervisor's note - Jeevan, chemistry department, Wednesday
Two students told me this week that Gopika, our research assistant, seems angry with everyone. They pointed to her jaw: clenched tight while she works, sometimes with a small grinding sound. One of them said, "She looks like she wants to bite someone."
I had noticed it too, but her words and actions were as polite as ever. She thanked people, shared equipment, stayed late.
On Tuesday I asked her to help me label samples and said, "You've seemed tense lately. Is everything okay?"
She touched her jaw, surprised. "Am I doing that again? I don't even notice." Then quietly: "My father has surgery next week, and I'm worried about the fees and about him."
I told her to take the time she needs, and pointed her to the student support office. I've asked the team not to read her jaw as anger.

qa.a: Next week.

qa.a: Gopika was worried and anxious about her father's surgery, not angry, and wasn't even aware of clenching her jaw.

I'm Leela, and I went with my friend Omkar to buy a second-hand laptop from a seller near Pune station. Omkar had practised the night before: keep a neutral face, don't look too eager.
When the seller named his price, Omkar's face didn't move at all. He said, "Hmm. I'll think."

I couldn't tell if the seller was offended or just bargaining.
Omkar noticed too. He kept his face calm but changed his words. "It's a good laptop. You've looked after it. I just have a student budget. Can we meet in the middle?"
The seller softened. They shook hands on a price both of them seemed okay with.

Subject: Paris and the Great Shrug

Baljeet,
Three weeks into the exchange and I finally understand something. Everyone here shrugs. The bakery lady shrugs. My flatmate shrugs. And in my first class, when I asked the professor whether the essay could be late, he shrugged, lips pushed out, and said, "Eh."
I was so hurt. I thought he was saying, "I couldn't care less about your problem." I didn't sleep well.
Next day I asked a French classmate. She laughed. "That shrug means 'it's possible, don't worry.' If he didn't care, he'd just say no."
I emailed him to check. He replied: "Of course, submit Friday."
So a shrug here can be friendly, casual, even kind. At home, if I shrugged at Papa, he'd think I was being rude.
I'm using words now. Much safer.
Nitin

Afterwards my mentor, Dr Hemant, said kindly, "Your research was excellent. But you looked like you were guarding it from us. The audience couldn't warm up to you."

- Rashmi

Trainer's note - Kavitha, corporate communication workshop, Thursday
Urmila, one of our graduate trainees, gave her first practice presentation today. Her content was strong. But for the full ten minutes, her arms were crossed stiffly, and when she wasn't crossing them, she gripped her elbows.
In the feedback round, two trainees said she seemed "not open to questions." Urmila frowned, a bit defensive. "I was just nervous."
I told her I believed that completely. Crossed arms often mean nerves or cold, not unfriendliness. But audiences can still read them as closed.
We practised together: arms relaxed at her sides, one hand pointing to the slides, palms up when inviting questions.
She tried again. The same trainees said she seemed "much more welcoming." Urmila laughed. "I'm exactly as nervous. It just doesn't show as much."
I reminded her: it's a skill, not a feeling. Confidence may come later.
